entities.name: Archibald Douglas, 5th Earl of Douglas
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Archibald Douglas, 5th Earl of Douglas and 2nd Duke of Touraine, emerged as a paramount figure in 15th-century Scotland, inheriting immense power and influence at a tumultuous time. Born around 1390, he succeeded his father, the formidable 4th Earl, after the latter’s death at the Battle of Verneuil in 1424, becoming one of the wealthiest and most militarily significant magnates in the kingdom. His career spanned the reigns of James I and James II, periods marked by fierce baronial rivalries, Anglo-Scottish tensions, and Scotland's complex involvement in the Hundred Years' War.

Douglas's early life saw him participate in the Franco-Scottish alliance, notably engaging in campaigns in France alongside his father. Upon his succession, he navigated the treacherous political landscape of James I's return from English captivity, initially aligning with the Crown but later facing royal suspicion due to his vast territorial holdings and independent military capabilities. He served as Lieutenant General of Scotland from 1437, following James I's assassination, and played a crucial role in the regency council for the young James II. His power was such that he effectively controlled much of southern Scotland, commanding a private army that rivaled the Crown's.

His death in 1439, possibly from plague, marked a significant turning point in Scottish politics. It removed a central pillar of the 'Black Douglas' power, paving the way for the young King James II to assert greater royal authority, though not without further conflict. The subsequent 'Black Dinner' of 1440, where his son and heir, William Douglas, 6th Earl of Douglas, was infamously murdered, directly led to the eventual forfeiture of the Douglas estates and the Crown's consolidation of power, fundamentally reshaping the balance between monarchy and nobility in Scotland.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Archibald Douglas's immense power as a magnate and his role in the regency following James I's death profoundly shaped Scottish politics, directly precipitating the Crown's struggle against the Douglas family that culminated in their eventual downfall. His career exemplifies the intense power struggles between the monarchy and the nobility in 15th-century Scotland.
